imageCaption: Aaliyah stands in the kitchen surrounded by open cookbooks, her hand-drawn diagrams, and ingredients in various states of organization. A blank recipe card sits in the center, waiting. Through the window behind her, the neighborhood is visible—early morning light, quiet streets.
text:
The first Sunday supper was in exactly six days.

Aaliyah knew this the way she knew her own heartbeat—not because she was checking constantly, but because the knowledge was already there, thrumming under everything else. Six days to figure out what to make. Six days to transform fourteen pieces of cardstock into an actual plan. Six days to prove that a neighborhood full of people who'd tasted one impossible meal wouldn't be disappointed by the second one.

She was, in other words, spiraling.

"You're doing the thing," Elijah announced, appearing in the kitchen doorway with the timing of someone who had developed a supernatural ability to sense when one of his siblings needed to be interrupted. "The thinking-so-hard-your-face-makes-that-shape thing."

"I am not," Aaliyah said, which was technically false because her face was definitely making a shape. "I'm planning."

"Same thing," Elijah said. He was carrying a rock he'd definitely found in the neighborhood—still had that specific New York sidewalk dust on it—and was apparently treating it as a consulting partner. "You're trying to solve the recipe like it's a math problem. Like there's a right answer hidden somewhere and you just have to find it."

"Isn't there?" Aaliyah gestured at the open cookbooks scattered across the kitchen table. She'd started with Dominican classics. Moved to fusion cuisine. Considered several recipes that probably required equipment they didn't have. Each one had seemed promising until she'd imagined serving it, and then she'd imagined the fourteen addresses on the invitation card, and then she'd imagined what they would taste like looking back on it, and then nothing seemed right.

"No," Elijah said with the confidence of a nine-year-old who'd apparently been thinking about this. "There's the answer that tastes right, and then there's all the other answers that are just... wrong in different ways. You've got to figure out which one tastes like home."

"Home is a flavor?" Aaliyah asked.

"Home is why you made the mofongo," Elijah corrected. He sat down at the table, still holding the rock like it was a small furry animal who might need comfort. "You didn't make it because it was traditional. You made it because Dad was excited about places, and Mom was trying to figure out why we stopped running, and I was trying to understand why Sully keeps barking at things nobody else can see. And it all went into the food because that's where feelings go when you're making something real."

This was, aggravating, completely correct.

"So I need to figure out what we're trying to say this week," Aaliyah said slowly.

"You need to figure out why we're saying it," Elijah corrected. "The first Sunday is about showing them who we are. The second Sunday should be about... what? What's the story we're telling now?"

Aaliyah thought about the invitation. The careful handwriting of at least four people. The specific request for chaos. The fourteen addresses of a neighborhood that had watched the Gomez family arrive unplanned and decided they wanted more of that.

"We're telling them it's not a one-time thing," she said. "We're telling them we're staying long enough to matter. We're telling them—" She paused, running her fingers over the edge of one of the cookbooks. "We're telling them that we're building something. Not just passing through."

Elijah nodded like she'd just solved a math problem he'd been waiting for her to understand. Which, she realized, she probably had.

"So it should be something that takes more than one Sunday to understand," he said. "Something that gets better the more times you eat it."

The back door opened and Anthony appeared, carrying coffee with the expression of a man who'd already been up for several hours and had thoughts about beverage science. "Your mother is showering and listening to something in Spanish very loudly," he announced. "I think she's mentally designing kitchen lighting. Is anyone else hungry?"

"Aaliyah's having a feelings spiral about recipes," Elijah reported. "But she just figured out that she needs to make something that's better on multiple Sundays instead of perfect on the first one."

Anthony sat down at the table without being invited, which meant this conversation was about to become a family affair. He took a long sip of his coffee. "So you need something that builds," he said. "Something that gets deeper the more you taste it."

"Exactly," Aaliyah said.

"Like a relationship," Anthony said. He had the expression of someone thinking very hard about something that had nothing to do with recipes. "You don't meet someone and know them completely. You meet them and then you taste their chaos again and again until one day you realize you love them because of all the details you've been slowly learning."

He pulled out his phone. "Marco's here. I invited him over to taste-test whatever you decide on. He texted that he's bringing 'opinions and judgment,' which in Marco vocabulary means he's very excited and also invested in making sure you understand the weight of what you're doing."

"That's not pressure," Aaliyah said. "That's just slightly terrifying."

"It's both," her father said cheerfully. "But here's the thing—Marco already thinks you're talented. This isn't a test of whether you can cook. It's a test of whether you understand why you're cooking. Those are different questions, and Marco's very good at asking the second one."

Sully appeared from wherever dogs went when they were thinking important thoughts, jumped directly into Elijah's lap without asking permission, and proceeded to steal the rock like he was a dog who understood that consulting partners should be rested.

"Okay," Aaliyah said. She pulled out a fresh piece of paper—the blank recipe card that had been sitting on the table waiting for her to decide. "I'm going to make something I have to taste on multiple Sundays to understand. Something that tastes different depending on when you eat it. Something that—"

She stopped. Because she'd just thought of something.

"Something that changes," she finished. "Like us. Like the neighborhood. Like—"

"Like Curaçao," Luisana said from the kitchen doorway, hair still wet, eyes bright with shower-steam and ideas. "Something seasonal. Something that's better in warm weather but has roots in places that are cold. Something that bridges."

She had her journal out, which meant this had officially become the kind of family conversation where breakfast turned into hours and nobody minded because the conversation was better than any meal they could schedule.

"Sancocho," Aaliyah said. "But not the traditional kind. The kind that adapts based on what the market has. The kind that's different every Sunday because the ingredients change."

"That's brilliant," Anthony said.

"That's adaptive," Luisana said, writing.

"That's exactly what we are," Elijah said, and Sully barked in agreement, still holding the consulting rock like it deserved credit for the insight.

And Aaliyah realized, writing the first ingredient on her card, that Elijah had been right. There wasn't a right recipe.

There was just the one that tasted like staying.

And she'd finally figured out what it was.
